'''''Genista monspessulana''''', commonly known as '''French broom''', '''Montpellier broom''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> or '''Cape broom''' (Australia), is a woody [[leguminous]] [[Perennial plant|perennial]] [[shrub]]. The yellow-flowering bush is native to the [[Mediterranean Region|Mediterranean region]], and while it may still be commonly sold in some garden stores, it is considered an [[invasive plant]] in most places where it has been introduced.<ref>Integrated Taxonomic Information System. [https://www.itis.gov/servlet/SingleRpt/SingleRpt?search_topic=TSN&search_value=502738 ''Genista monspessulana''], webpage for taxonomic serial number 502738 retrieved May 19, 2007.</ref> It is a [[noxious weed]] on the western coast of the US and in parts of Australia.

==Description==

''G. monspessulana'' grows to {{convert|1-2.5|m|ft|abbr=off|frac=2}} tall, with slender green branches. Stems generally ridged or angled and green when young.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |title=The Jepson Manual, Vascular Plants of California |publisher=University of California Press |year=2012 |isbn=9780520253124 |editor-last=Baldwin |editor-first=B.G. |edition=2nd |location=Berkeley, California |publication-date=2012 |pages=754 |language=English |editor-last2=Goldman |editor-first2=D.H.}}</ref> The [[leaves]] are [[evergreen]], [[trifoliate]] with three narrow [[obovate]] leaflets, {{convert|1|–|2|cm|abbr=off|frac=4}} long. The [[flower]]s are yellow, grouped 3–9 together in short [[raceme]]s. Like other [[Fabaceae|legumes]], it develops its seeds within a pod. The pods are {{Convert|2–3|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long, tough and hard, covered all over with hairs,<ref name=":0" /> and are transported easily by flowing water and animals. They burst open with force, dispersing the seeds several metres. The plant begins seed production once it reaches a height of approximately {{convert|40|cm|abbr=on}}, and each plant can live for 10–20 years. One mature plant can produce 10,000 seeds per season. The generous seed production and the plant's ability to re-sprout after cutting or burning help it to invade new habitat vigorously when introduced.<ref name="Bossard">{{cite book|author=Bossard, Carla|year=2000|title="''Genista Monspessulana''," in ''Invasive Plants of California's Wildlands''|editor=Carla C. Bossard|editor2=John M. Randall|editor3=Marc C. Hoshovsky|publisher=[[University of California]]|place=[[Berkeley, California|Berkeley]]|isbn=978-0-520-22546-6|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/invasiveplantsof00carl}}</ref><ref name="ANR">{{cite journal|author=D'Antonio, Carla|year=2007|url=http://ucce.ucdavis.edu/datastore/detailreport.cfm?usernumber=52&surveynumber=182|title=''Genista monspessulana''|journal=Agriculture and Natural Resources|publisher= University of California|accessdate=May 19, 2007}}</ref><ref name="Hoshovsky">{{cite web |author=Hoshovsky, Marc |year=1986 |url=http://tncweeds.ucdavis.edu/esadocs/documnts/cytisco.pdf |title=Element Stewardship Abstract for ''Cytisus scoparius'' and ''Genista monspessulanus'' |publisher=[[The Nature Conservancy]] |place=Arlington |accessdate=May 19, 2007 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20061126052334/http://tncweeds.ucdavis.edu/esadocs/documnts/cytisco.pdf |archivedate=November 26, 2006 }}</ref>

It is related to the [[common broom]] and [[Spartium junceum|Spanish broom]].

==Distribution and habitat==
''G. monspessulana'' and related plants are common in European [[shrubland]]s. French broom was originally distributed throughout Mediterranean [[Europe]] and northwest [[Africa]], the [[Azores]], and the [[Canary Islands]].<ref name="Hoshovsky" /> Due to its lower tolerance for [[frost]] than other broom species, it is common in warmer, lower elevation areas. It is found on coastal strips and in sunny inland areas, and does best with plentiful rainfall and sandy soils.

==Ecology==
When introduced to a new area, French broom can become an [[invasive plant]]. Its reproductive vigour and preference for [[Mediterranean climate]]s make it a very successful species in [[California]] and the [[Pacific Northwest]], where it is considered a severe [[noxious weed]], covering over 40 kilo[[hectare]]s.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://portal.cal-ipc.org/files/PAFs/Genista%20monspessulana.pdf |title=Genista monspessulana |publisher=[[California Invasive Plant Council]] |accessdate=May 17, 2007 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070802120534/http://portal.cal-ipc.org/files/PAFs/Genista%20monspessulana.pdf |archivedate=August 2, 2007 }}</ref> It is even more widespread in Australia, where it covers 600 kilohectares and is also considered a noxious weed.<ref>{{cite web|publisher=[[Australian Weeds Committee]] |year=2007 |url=http://www.weeds.org.au/docs/weednet6.pdf |title=Noxious Weed List for Australian States and Territories |work=Cooperative Research Center for Australian Weed Management |accessdate=May 19, 2007 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20070830083549/http://www.weeds.org.au/docs/weednet6.pdf |archivedate=August 30, 2007 }}</ref>

The plant often outcompetes [[native vegetation]], forming dense fields where other species are almost completely crowded out. Stands of French broom can be so thick that they make meadows and pastures useless for wild and domestic animals. It can also shade out tree seedlings in [[reforested]] areas and tends to catch fire.<ref name="Hoshovsky"/>

==Toxicity==

The leaves and seeds contain [[alkaloid]]s which are poisonous to many large domestic animals.<ref name="Hoshovsky"/>
